representativeSnapshot.kind: Static review of the full org_role_permissions history in the active chain, plus EXECUTED two-layer evidence on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster. THE DEFECT IS REAL AND MEASURED, NOT ASSERTED. The chain seeds FIVE roles (20250816132000:44-49 owner/admin/production/finance and 20260712005429:219-235 tour_manager) and NONE of them carries a workforce.* permission: 20260821180438:81-95 added workforce.view / workforce.manage / workforce.publish to the PER-MEMBER org_members.permissions CHECK constraint and to no role at all. The harness reproduces that matrix from the chain's own bytes, asserts has_perm returns false for all three workforce permissions for all five seeded roles (15 measurements), and then measures the split-brain as three independent facts about ONE identity: layer 1, the REAL resolveEffectiveAdminCapabilities over the matrix row, says an org admin HAS workforce.view and workforce.manage; layer 2, the chain's own public.has_perm, says it has NEITHER; and the consequence, the chain's own staff_members_scoped_read, returns ZERO of org A's three staff rows to that caller while org A demonstrably has them. That is a plausible zero arriving through authorization, which CP-098 forbids and which a denial would have made legible. AFTER: 64 PASS / 0 FAIL, exit 0, deterministic across two runs. The two layers agree on all 36 (role, workforce permission) pairs. EXECUTED NEGATIVE CONTROLS, because a green assertion nobody has seen fail is not evidence: the migration's own post-condition is proven able to fire FIVE different ways (CP-094 negative, additivity, seed arity, seed vocabulary, target drift), each leaving the matrix byte-identical so the post-condition is provably INSIDE the transaction; the two-layer comparator is proven able to report a disagreement before it is trusted with a zero; the vitest catalog-vs-seed comparison is proven able to fail by pointing it at a tampered copy of the migration; and the read-only postflight is proven able to fail four different ways.

assumptions: The repository's role list is EXACTLY the twelve roles ROLE_DEFAULT_CAPABILITIES defines (lib/auth/admin-capabilities.ts:123-138) and the handoff's per-role table matches it. VERIFIED, not assumed: __tests__/admin/db016-capability-matrix-agreement.test.ts re-derives the seed from the live catalog with WFC-003's own deriveWorkforceRoleSeedDecisions (types/vendor-identity-contract.ts:830-860) and compares it to the literal parsed out of the migration file, so an ADMIN-012 change to any role's capabilities turns this suite red until WFC-003 re-decides. No role was invented and no role from the brief was dropped.

CP-102's subtraction is load-bearing and is NOT redesigned here: has_perm(uid, oid, perm) has no target argument (20260821180438:122-151), so ANY permission in org_role_permissions is granted across the whole organization. workforce.manage is department-scoped for department_manager (lib/auth/admin-capabilities.ts:319-323) and is therefore withheld from the matrix. workforce.view and workforce.publish are NOT department-scoped (ADMIN-012's explicit decision, same file :304-313) and are seeded, organization-wide. That residual is WFC-005/WFC-006's.

THE THREE workforce.* PERMISSIONS ARE THE WHOLE VOCABULARY. Read from the chain, not restated: the migration asserts that each of the three appears in the rendered text of public.org_members.org_members_permissions_check (20260821180438:81-96) and that the constraint is VALID, so a typo and a future vocabulary change are both caught at apply time. The equality assertion is then scoped to those three names rather than to the workforce.% prefix, so a future fourth workforce permission in a later migration cannot make THIS file's post-condition un-satisfiable on a legitimate target.

This migration changes DATA in one existing table and NO table, column, index, constraint, trigger, policy or function. lib/database.types.ts therefore needs NO regeneration: the generated contract describes shape and no shape changed. Regeneration is separately blocked anyway (CP-089, CP-092, HF-DB-008-REGENERATION-UNREACHABLE-AND-LINKED-TARGET-IS-A-DIFFERENT-DATABASE) and the `linked` project is a DIFFERENT database that must never be regenerated from.

A role that has no matrix row is created with just its declared slice. For ticketing, ticketing_manager and worker that slice is empty, so the inserted row is perms = '{}'. That is behaviourally identical to the absent row it replaces: has_perm coalesces a missing matrix row to an empty array (20260821180438:148) and admin_current_acting_context does the same (20260722002848:290). The rows are created so the matrix is self-describing and so the post-condition can distinguish 'this role was measured and holds nothing' from 'this role was never examined'. NO ROW IS CREATED WITH ANY PERMISSION IT WAS NOT GRANTED BY THE RULE.

perms is written as a sorted, de-duplicated union. array_agg(DISTINCT ...) is load-bearing rather than cosmetic: without it the union keeps a permission the target already held, the exact-membership assertion correctly refuses, and the migration is not idempotent because its own post-condition aborts the second apply. Found by this lane's own harness on its first run; recorded because it is the kind of thing that reads as a tidy-up.

The union lives in the ON CONFLICT clause and NOT in the SELECT list. PostgreSQL does not put the target table in scope for `insert ... select`: referencing org_role_permissions.perms in the SELECT list is SQLSTATE 42P01 'invalid reference to FROM-clause entry'. Also found by this lane's own harness on its first run.

capability_version DIGESTS THE ARRAY IN ORDER. admin_acting_context_sessions.capability_version is encode(digest(concat_ws('|', v_role, array_to_string(v_perms, ',')), 'sha256'), 'hex') (20260722002848:180-183) and the same expression is re-checked on EVERY use (20260722002848:317-320). Writing the sorted form therefore changes the digest for every role this file touches EVEN FOR PERMISSIONS THAT WERE ALREADY GRANTED, because the array is re-ordered. admin_current_acting_context recomputes the digest from the same expression, so the sort is behaviourally inert; it is stated because an operator reasoning about which sessions break needs the exact rule, and 'only the new permissions change it' is the wrong answer.

THE SPLIT-BRAIN IS CLOSED FOR THE workforce.* FAMILY ONLY, AND THE REST IS MEASURED, NOT ABSORBED. After this migration the residual superset pairs (application gate grants, matrix does not) across the WHOLE 42-capability catalog are 206, per role: owner=37 admin=35 tour_manager=26 production=24 production_manager=24 department_manager=11 finance=13 finance_manager=14 ticketing=7 ticketing_manager=7 viewer=9 worker=0. The workforce family's share of that is exactly 0. The rest is the matrix carrying the legacy staff.manage / event.manage vocabulary and none of the other 39 capabilities, and it is a NEW decision reserved to WFC-003 under a new CP (HF-WFC-004-WORKFORCE-RBAC-PROVISIONING residual gap #1). Widening the seed to the full catalog projection from inside this migration would have been a silent workforce-identity decision made by a security lane.

Per-TENANT delegation stays configuration and is NOT authored here. The existing mechanism is the per-member org_members.permissions array, already constrained to the capability catalog by org_members_permissions_check and unioned by has_perm (same file :143-149). No second membership table, no second role table and no new permission vocabulary were introduced. has_perm + org_members + org_role_permissions is the whole model.

isOrganizationCreator / isMasterAccount return ALL_CAPABILITIES in the resolver (lib/auth/admin-capabilities.ts:462) and bypass has_perm entirely, so such a caller with no org_members row is authorized at the route and still reads nothing. UNCHANGED, and deliberately so: the correct remedy is a membership row, not a new RLS bypass. Both harnesses measure the organization-level projection with neither flag set, because that is the only projection the two layers can be compared on.

workforce.publish is seeded for eight roles but NO RLS POLICY READS IT ANYWHERE IN THE CHAIN: a full-text scan for 'workforce.publish' in supabase/migrations returns the CHECK constraint at 20260821180438:88 and nothing else. It is granted so the two vocabularies agree and so the route gate at app/api/admin/events/[id]/work-mode/route.ts:32 has a matrix counterpart; it currently changes no row-level access. Recorded so nobody reads the seed as a claim that publish is enforced at the database.
layeredPlan: Layer 0 (PREFLIGHT, read-only, operator). Run preflight.rowCountQueries. Three things decide whether this file is correct for THIS target: (a) the full current org_role_permissions matrix - if any role already carries a workforce.* permission this rule does not grant it, the migration's exact-membership assertion will ABORT the apply, and that is a stop condition to route back, not to work around; (b) whether any admin_acting_context_sessions rows exist, because this apply invalidates every one of them and the re-activation path must be verified BEFORE the apply, not after; (c) has_perm('authenticated', ...) is not applicable - has_perm is SECURITY DEFINER and is granted to authenticated at 20260711153040:36, so record has_function_privilege anyway, because a missing EXECUTE grant makes every workforce RLS predicate error rather than deny and the operator should know that is a different failure from a denial.

Layer 1 (apply, single run, operator). One transaction, explicit, this file only - never `supabase db reset`, never `db push --include-all`, never a chain replay (CP-051). A DO block that: asserts the table and the text[] NOT NULL column shape; asserts org_members_permissions_check exists and is VALID and admits all three workforce permissions; snapshots the matrix as JSONb; asserts the seed literal holds exactly 12 roles; upserts all twelve roles with a sorted de-duplicated union; asserts no pre-existing permission was removed; asserts no role outside the declared seed was created; asserts department_manager does not carry workforce.manage, by name and with the CP-094 reason in the message; asserts the seed names nothing outside the governed vocabulary; and asserts each role's workforce.* slice EQUALS the declared slice. The post-condition is inside the same transaction as the write, so a target that cannot reach the asserted state fails the apply instead of reporting success.

Layer 2 (postflight, read-only, operator). Run supabase/tests/db016_workforce_role_seed_contract.sql; expect zero violation rows and exactly one summary row rendering `DB-016 workforce role seed|t`. Then the six probes in postflight.queries, each labelled with WHICH identity ran it, because a probe run as the wrong identity is not evidence. The probes that matter most are the two-layer ones: an organization administrator who reads 0 rows is a FAILED apply, and a department_manager who can UPDATE org rows is a CP-094 violation.

Layer 3 (no fourth layer in this lane). Five things are routed rather than absorbed: the 206-pair residual outside the workforce family (WFC-003, new CP); the seven matrix-less roles' non-workforce authority (same); the organization-wide `workforce.view` for department_manager (WFC-005/WFC-006); the isOrganizationCreator / isMasterAccount bypass (unchanged by design); and CI wiring for the two instruments, which exist and are proven but run on nobody's behalf because package.json and .github/workflows/ are outside this lane's grant and DB-015 owns scripts/ci/.

rowCountQueries: SELECT role, perms FROM public.org_role_permissions ORDER BY role
SELECT r.role, p.perm FROM public.org_role_permissions r, unnest(r.perms) AS p(perm) WHERE p.perm LIKE 'workforce.%' ORDER BY r.role, p.perm
SELECT count(*) AS acting_context_sessions, count(*) FILTER (WHERE revoked_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now()) AS live_sessions FROM public.admin_acting_context_sessions
SELECT c.relrowsecurity, c.relforcerowsecurity FROM pg_class c JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace WHERE n.nspname = 'public' AND c.relname IN ('org_role_permissions','org_members')
SELECT conname, convalidated, pg_get_constraintdef(oid) FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'public.org_members'::regclass AND conname = 'org_members_permissions_check'
SELECT policyname, polcmd, polpermissive, polroles::regrole[], qual FROM pg_policies WHERE schemaname = 'public' AND tablename = 'org_role_permissions' ORDER BY policyname
preflight.expectedAffectedRows: At most 12 rows in public.org_role_permissions are touched, and they are TOUCHED not replaced: every write is a sorted de-duplicated union of the row's existing perms and the declared slice, so a role that already held its slice is rewritten byte-identically and a role with no row is created with its slice. On a target matching the chain, 5 rows are updated (owner, admin, production, finance, tour_manager) and 7 are inserted (production_manager, finance_manager, viewer, department_manager, ticketing, ticketing_manager, worker). Every pre-existing permission survives. No table, column, index, constraint, trigger, policy or function is created, altered or dropped, and no other table's row is read for update or deleted.

execution.resumeStrategy: Authored - manual apply pending (CP-051). One transaction, one file, all twelve roles in ONE migration so a single re-activation covers the whole change. The write is 12 single-row upserts on a table that currently holds five rows and will hold at most seventeen; `set local lock_timeout = '5s'` is set in the file. No table is rewritten, re-indexed or re-vacuumed, so there is no lock-budget risk from the data side. Safe to apply BEFORE any consumer change: the write is a union, so no caller loses a permission it held. The only behaviour that changes is that callers who previously received a plausible zero now receive rows - which is the point - and that every active acting-context session is invalidated, which is why re-activation verification is a PREFLIGHT step.
execution.idempotency: Deterministic and repeatable. `insert ... on conflict (role) do update set perms = <sorted de-duplicated union>` is a set union, so applying twice is a no-op; the sorted form makes the resulting array byte-identical across applies rather than merely equivalent. Verified by applying the file twice on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster in supabase/tests/db016_workforce_role_seed.harness.sh: no error, and the rendered matrix was byte-identical before and after. The in-transaction post-condition is what makes that true rather than accidental: an earlier revision of this file omitted DISTINCT from the union, which produced a duplicated permission, which the post-condition correctly refused - so the second apply aborted. Both defects were found by the harness, not by reading.
execution.in_transaction_post_condition: Asserted, not assumed: the table and text[] NOT NULL column shape; org_members_permissions_check present, VALID and admitting all three workforce permissions; the seed literal holding exactly 12 roles; NO pre-existing permission removed (measured against a JSONb snapshot of the target's real pre-state); no role created outside the declared seed; department_manager NOT carrying workforce.manage; the seed naming nothing outside the governed vocabulary; and each role's workforce.* slice EQUALING the declared slice. Five of these are proven able to fail by the harness.

quarantine.strategy: No data movement, no backfill, no batch. The change is at most twelve single-row upserts on one existing table. There is no partial-application state: the file is one transaction and its own post-condition RAISEs if the asserted state is unreachable, so a half-applied matrix cannot be committed. The snapshot it compares against is a plpgsql variable, not a temporary table, so nothing is left behind in any schema on commit.
quarantine.lockBudget: org_role_permissions has a `role text primary key` (20250816132000:40) and currently five rows. The write takes one row lock per role, held to the end of the transaction. No hot path reads this table FOR UPDATE: `admin_current_acting_context` takes a plain left join (20260722002848:302) and `roleperms_select ... using (true)` makes the whole matrix readable by anyone, which is a disclosure posture CP-102 accepted deliberately rather than a concurrency risk. The sub-selects in the post-condition read the same 12 rows twice and are trivially cheap.

constraints: No constraint is added, altered or dropped. org_role_permissions_role_key (the primary key) and org_members_permissions_check are untouched; the latter is READ, and the migration refuses to apply if it is absent or NOT VALID.

THE AUTHORIZATION CONSEQUENCE IS THE WHOLE POINT. public.org_role_permissions IS the authority every workforce-governed RLS predicate reads through has_perm(uid, oid, perm) - staff_members_scoped_read/_insert/_update (20260926150000:173-197), staff_shifts_scoped_* (20260821031214:125-170), the staff-zone and site-map helpers (20260903120000:782-783, :1793-1826) and the tour-collaboration policies (20260720020544:215-322). Adding workforce.view to nine roles and workforce.manage to five therefore widens WHO can read organization-scoped workforce rows. That widening is bounded to the owning organization by the org_id conjunct those policies already carry, and the harness proves it: for all twelve roles, a member of org A reads org A's rows and ZERO of org B's.

The five roles that gain workforce.manage are exactly the organization-wide ones, and workforce.manage is the permission that permits INSERT and UPDATE on staff_members (20260926150000:197, :220). So this migration does widen write access for five roles inside the organization. That is CP-094's own sentence - 'Organization administrators retain organization-wide workforce authority' - applied to tour_manager, production and production_manager by WFC-003's rule, and it is the reason the apply is reviewed by security-admin rather than accepted on the harness alone.

The matrix remains world-readable through roleperms_select ... using (true) (20250816132000:112). This migration does not add a read policy and does not restrict that one; the contract postflight asserts the policy is still there, so that this file cannot quietly become a new configuration surface or a new disclosure. Stated because it is a real posture: after this apply, anyone can read which role carries which workforce capability.
indexes: No index is added. The primary key on `role` (20250816132000:40) serves the ON CONFLICT lookup, and the post-condition's per-role lookups are the same single-row probe. A twelve-row table needs nothing else.
constraintsAndIndexes.validationPlan: supabase/tests/db016_workforce_role_seed_contract.sql returns violation rows only, plus one summary row `DB-016 workforce role seed|t` computed from the same predicates, so an unapplied target cannot pass vacuously - measured: on a target holding the chain's own pre-state it returns 8 violation rows and summary `f`. It asserts 9 properties: the perms column shape; org_members_permissions_check present and VALID; all 12 role rows present; each role's workforce.* slice equal to the declared slice, per role so the row names which role disagreed; THE CP-094 NEGATIVE on its own, so a violation is reported as a rule violation rather than as a data mismatch; owner and admin still carry staff.manage; the five organization-wide roles carry workforce.manage; the three no-authority roles carry none; no role holds a workforce.* permission outside the governed three; and the matrix is still world-readable through roleperms_select. It is proven able to fail FOUR ways (admin loses workforce.manage, department_manager gains it, owner loses staff.manage, a role row is missing), and the harness additionally proves the MIGRATION ITSELF refuses a drifted target, which is the stronger claim.
constraintsAndIndexes.behaviouralPlan: supabase/tests/db016_workforce_role_seed.harness.sh, EXECUTED to ALL CHECKS PASSED, 64 PASS / 0 FAIL, exit 0, on a throwaway PostgreSQL 16.15 cluster, twice with identical output. It extracts the chain's own organizations / org_members / org_role_permissions / staff_members DDL, public.has_perm, public.is_org_member, org_members_permissions_check and the staff_members_scoped_read / _update / _worker_read_own policies BY LINE RANGE at run time, so the emulated authority cannot drift from the chain. It then: asserts the chain-HEAD pre-state (5 roles, zero workforce permissions, 15 false has_perm answers, org A holding 3 staff rows so a zero is measurable); measures the live split-brain as three independent facts about one identity; proves its own comparator can report a disagreement; proves five distinct in-transaction post-conditions can fire, each leaving the matrix byte-identical; proves the unmodified migration still applies from the same restored state; asserts has_perm over all 36 (role, permission) pairs; asserts the department_manager negative on its own; diffs perms per role for removals; reads org A and org B row counts for all twelve roles; proves idempotence; exports the measured matrix, has_perm answers and row reads to JSON and runs the REAL TypeScript resolver over them, comparing all 36 pairs and measuring the 206-pair residual outside the workforce family; runs the vitest agreement test both with and without the database fixture, including a negative control that points it at a tampered migration; runs the contract postflight and proves it can fail four ways with the matrix restored around each probe; and re-asserts its own post-state. It HARD-ABORTS on any fixture-stage failure rather than continuing, because a silently failed fixture is the Wave 33 failure shape.

recovery.rollback: ISSUE AS A LATER FORWARD MIGRATION, never as an edit to this file. The matrix is data, so a rollback is a data write: for each of the twelve roles, `UPDATE public.org_role_permissions SET perms = <the pre-apply perms array>` using the preflight snapshot in the operator manifest, which is why the preflight capture matters. A blunt `perms = array_remove(perms, 'workforce.*')` is NOT a rollback: it would also strip any workforce permission the target legitimately held beforehand, which the migration's own additivity assertion exists to prevent. NOTE THAT ROLLING BACK RE-OPENS THE DEFECT: a legitimate organization administrator will again pass withAdminCapability('workforce.manage') and again read zero rows. The preferred recovery for a bad apply is therefore a forward fix, not this rollback.
recovery.forwardFix: Any correction is a new additive migration with a higher version carrying another union upsert. Two things make a forward fix safe: the union form means a forward fix cannot remove anything, and this file's post-condition will raise on a forward fix that leaves a drifted workforce slice behind. The one correction that is NOT available as a forward fix is adding workforce.manage to department_manager - the post-condition refuses it, by design, and CP-094 is the reason.

queries: SELECT role, perms FROM public.org_role_permissions ORDER BY role

-- A CORRECT OUTCOME LOOKS LIKE THIS. Run each as a real caller with that caller's own JWT; label the result with WHICH identity ran it. (1) THE HEADLINE PROBE, an organization administrator (role owner or admin) of the owning organization: SELECT count(*) FROM public.staff_members; -> returns that organization's row count, NOT 0. This is the probe that matches the defect, and 0 here is a FAILED APPLY, not a correct denial: the caller passed the route gate and must now receive rows. app/api/admin/staff/route.ts:17 is gated on workforce.view and reads exactly this.

-- (2) THE WRITE PROBE, as the same administrator: pick a row in your own organization and UPDATE a benign column. -> UPDATE 1. UPDATE 0 means workforce.manage did not land and the apply is incomplete.

-- (3) THE CP-094 PROBE, as a department_manager: SELECT count(*) FROM public.staff_members WHERE org_id = '<your org>'; -> returns your organization's row count (workforce.view is organization-wide for this role). Then UPDATE one of those rows. -> UPDATE 0. UPDATE 1 IS A CP-094 VIOLATION: stop, roll forward, and page security-admin. This is the single change that would actually violate CP-094, and it is why the migration asserts its absence in-transaction rather than trusting review.

-- (4) CROSS-TENANT, as any caller holding workforce.view or workforce.manage: SELECT count(*) FROM public.staff_members WHERE org_id = '<an organization you are not a member of>'; -> returns 0. The query SUCCEEDS; 0 rows, not a permission error. An `ERROR: permission denied for table staff_members` here means the GRANT is missing, which is a different problem and not a pass.

-- (5) THE NO-WIDENING PROBE, as the same administrator: SELECT count(*) FROM public.staff_members WHERE org_id = '<another organization>'; -> 0. This is the probe that proves the seed widened WHO can read inside an organization and not ACROSS organizations. If it returns rows, stop.

-- (6) THE VOCABULARY PROBE, read-only: SELECT r.role, p.perm FROM public.org_role_permissions r, unnest(r.perms) p(perm) WHERE p.perm LIKE 'workforce.%' ORDER BY r.role, p.perm; -> exactly the expected 19 rows and no others: 5 roles x 3 permissions (view, manage, publish) + 3 roles x 1 (finance, finance_manager, viewer) + 1 role x 2 (department_manager) + 3 roles x 0. If department_manager appears with workforce.manage, stop.

-- (7) THE SESSION PROBE, read-only, and the reason the preflight asked for it: SELECT count(*) FROM public.admin_acting_context_sessions WHERE revoked_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now(); -> every one of these sessions is now INVALID, because capability_version digests org_role_permissions.perms (20260722002848:180-183, re-checked at :317-320). Each affected user must re-activate their acting context. Attach the number to the release ticket so support knows what to expect.
